questions.question: Charles Darwin set out natural selection in On the Origin of Species in 1859, and ten years later he took up Herbert Spencer's phrase for it, survival of the fittest. Four stags share one wood: one wins the most fights, one fathers the most fawns, one runs the fastest and one lives the longest. Which stag does a biologist call the fittest?
questions.answer: The one that fathers the most fawns
choices: The one that fathers the most fawns
The one that wins the most fights
The one that runs the fastest
The one that lives the longest
questions.context: To a biologist, fitness means how many young an animal leaves to carry its traits on; strength, speed and a long life count only as far as they help it breed. A stag that wins every fight but fathers no fawns passes none of his traits to the next generation. Darwin's idea is that living things whose inherited traits suit their surroundings leave more young, so those traits grow more common, generation after generation.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names natural selection as Darwin's idea, and fitness as leaving young (not strength) is the standard way it is explained.

questions.question: Charles Darwin kept every breed of pigeon he could buy and joined two London pigeon clubs. A fantail pigeon spreads thirty or even forty tail feathers, where other pigeons have twelve or fourteen, and many breeds look as different from one another as wild species do. Where did Darwin conclude that all the breeds had come from?
questions.answer: One wild species, for all the breeds
choices: One wild species, for all the breeds
A different wild species for each breed
Two wild species, crossed long ago
Several wild species, crossed together
questions.context: Darwin concluded that every breed came from one wild bird, the rock pigeon, changed by breeders who chose which birds to mate, generation after generation; he called this "man's power of accumulative selection." Most pigeon fanciers he met were sure that each main breed came from its own wild species. His book On the Origin of Species opens with such breeds, to show how far choosing can change a living thing.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade accounts of Darwin tell how breeders' artificial selection, his pigeons above all, led him to natural selection.

questions.question: Ivory hunters killed about nine in ten of the elephants in Gorongosa National Park, in Mozambique, during years of war. A few female elephants are born with no tusks at all. Before the war, nearly one female in five was tuskless; by 2000, about half of them were. What best explains the change?
questions.answer: Tuskless females were spared and passed the trait on
choices: Tuskless females were spared and passed the trait on
Females stopped growing tusks to escape the hunters
Each female's tusks shrank as the hunting went on
Fear of the hunters stunted the tusks of the young
questions.context: Hunters shot elephants for their tusks, so tuskless females were far more likely to survive and have young, and tusklessness is inherited. No elephant changed her own tusks: the herd changed because of which elephants lived to breed, which is why biologists say that populations evolve, not individuals.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that natural selection changes a population over generations, not one animal in its lifetime, and applies it to new cases like this one.

questions.question: Wild cabbage, a weedy plant of the mustard family, grows on seaside cliffs in western Europe. Farmers bred it into several vegetables by saving seed, generation after generation, from the plants with the most of whatever part they wanted to eat. Which vegetable came from choosing plants with the biggest clusters of flower buds?
choices: Broccoli
Cabbage
Kohlrabi
Brussels sprouts
questions.context: A head of broccoli is a crowd of unopened flower buds on thick stalks, and cauliflower came from the flower clusters too. Kale came from choosing big leaves, cabbage from the big bud at the tip of the plant, kohlrabi from a swollen stalk and Brussels sprouts from the small buds along its side. Many textbooks call the wild plant wild mustard, and all these vegetables still belong to its one species.
questions.grade_note: The wild-mustard family of vegetables is the standard seventh-grade example of artificial selection.

questions.question: Dogs range from the Chihuahua, under 3 kilograms, to the Great Dane, over 70, all shaped by people choosing which dogs to breed. Robert Wayne's team compared the DNA of dogs with that of wolves, coyotes and jackals in the 1990s. Which ancestry did the DNA show?
questions.answer: Wolves alone, for small and large breeds alike
choices: Wolves alone, for small and large breeds alike
Jackals for small breeds, wolves for large ones
Wolves, coyotes and jackals, all mixed together
Coyotes for some breeds, wolves for the rest
questions.context: Dog DNA was far closer to wolves' than to coyotes' or jackals', so dogs descend from an ancient population of wolves, tamed at least 15,000 years ago. Charles Darwin had thought that wolves, coyotes and jackals might all have played a part, and Konrad Lorenz, a famous student of animal behaviour, thought some breeds came from jackals. The breeds themselves are the work of artificial selection.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade gives dog breeds bred from wolves as a main example of artificial selection.

questions.question: Corn comes from teosinte, a wild grass of Mexico whose small ears hold about a dozen kernels or fewer, each sealed in a stony case. A change in one gene leaves a teosinte kernel bare. Over thousands of years, farmers there turned the grass into corn with bare kernels. What was the farmers' part in it?
questions.answer: Planting seed from the plants with the change
choices: Planting seed from the plants with the change
Cracking the cases until plants stopped making them
Roasting the seeds until the gene itself changed
Crossing the grass with wheat to bring the change in
questions.context: The farmers could not make the change happen; it arose by chance in a few plants, and by planting more of the seed they liked, they made it common. That choosing, generation after generation, is artificial selection, and it began in southwestern Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Cracked cases are not inherited, and wheat reached the Americas only when Europeans brought it, thousands of years later.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade gives crops bred from wild ancestors, corn from teosinte among them, as examples of artificial selection.

questions.question: Doctors cleared a woman's chest infection twice with the same antibiotic. The third time, the drug barely worked, and tests in the hospital laboratory showed that her infection now resisted it. What had become resistant, and how?
questions.answer: The bacteria, as resistant ones lived and multiplied
choices: The bacteria, as resistant ones lived and multiplied
Her body, as it grew used to the drug over the years
The bacteria, as each one learned to stand the drug
Her immune system, as it began to fight the drug off
questions.context: Each dose killed the bacteria the drug could kill, and the few that could resist it lived and multiplied, passing their resistance on, so the infection came back resistant. No bacterium learns to resist, and a person's body never becomes resistant to an antibiotic, though a World Health Organization survey in 2015 found that three people in four thought it did.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask students to apply natural selection to new cases, and antibiotic resistance is the usual one.

questions.question: A new chemical spray for killing insects came into wide use in the 1940s, and at first it worked well against houseflies. By 1947, flies in parts of Europe were surviving it, and the spraying was failing. Why could resistance spread through the flies so quickly?
questions.answer: Flies raise many generations in a single year
choices: Flies raise many generations in a single year
Each fly grew tougher after its first dose
The spray changed the flies' genes to resist it
Flies are so small that the poison wears off
questions.context: The spray was DDT. Natural selection works from one generation to the next, and a housefly can grow from egg to adult in about ten days, so flies pass through ten or more generations a year; each spraying left the rare flies that could survive it to breed, and their young inherited the resistance. More than 500 kinds of insect have since evolved resistance to some pesticide.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade applies natural selection to insects resisting a pesticide and explains why fast breeders change fast.

questions.question: Bernard Kettlewell marked pale and dark peppered moths with a dot of paint under the wings and set them free in a wood near Birmingham, where soot had blackened the bark. Later he trapped as many as he could. Then he did the same in a clean wood in Dorset, its bark pale with lichen. What did he find?
questions.answer: Those that matched the bark came back more often
choices: Those that matched the bark came back more often
Dark ones came back more often in both woods
Pale ones came back more often in both woods
Both kinds came back about equally in each wood
questions.context: In each wood he recaptured about twice as many, or more, of the moths that matched the bark: birds hunting by sight had eaten more of the ones that stood out, and Niko Tinbergen filmed birds taking them. The dark form had been rare before factory soot blackened the woods, yet by 1895 it made up about 98 moths in 100 around Manchester.
questions.grade_note: The peppered moth is the classic seventh-grade example of natural selection, and Kettlewell's two woods are its first test.

questions.question: Critics said Bernard Kettlewell had set his peppered moths on bare tree trunks, far more crowded than in the wild. Michael Majerus tested it again for six years in his garden near Cambridge, where the air had long been clean. Each night he let a dozen moths settle on branches, as wild ones mostly do, and at dawn he watched for birds. What did he find?
questions.answer: Birds ate more of the dark moths than the pale
choices: Birds ate more of the dark moths than the pale
Birds ate more of the pale moths than the dark
Birds ate the dark and pale moths about equally
Bats, not birds, ate nearly all of the moths
questions.context: Nine kinds of bird, robins and blue tits among them, took the dark moths more often, as Kettlewell had found in clean woods, and over those years the dark form near Cambridge fell from about 12 moths in 100 to 1. Majerus died in 2009, and four colleagues published his results in 2012 as the most direct evidence yet that birds drive the change. A 2002 book's charge that Kettlewell had cheated was examined by scientists and found to be without merit.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade accounts of the peppered moth now add Majerus's re-test, which answered the critics and confirmed the result.
